meta.topic: Build a RAG App with LlamaIndex
meta.title: Build a RAG App with LlamaIndex
meta.thesis: Build a RAG App with LlamaIndex is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A LlamaIndex onboarding assistant must answer handbook questions with page-level evidence. By the end, they should be able to build or review LlamaIndex index, query engine, and citation validation plan, measure answer groundedness and source coverage, and catch the failure where metadata is lost, so answers cannot point back to the handbook section.

mentalMap.title: Build a RAG App with LlamaIndex: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Build a LlamaIndex RAG slice around readers, nodes, indexes, retrievers, query engines, source nodes, and retrieval evaluation.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: A LlamaIndex RAG app should make the data path explicit: source documents become nodes, nodes become indexed evidence, and query engines return inspectable source nodes.

modules.title: Pin the query-engine contract
modules.sub: Start with the answer behavior a LlamaIndex query engine must satisfy.
modules.summary: The first LlamaIndex build target is a trustworthy query engine over a tiny corpus.
objectives: Explain why pin the query-engine contract matters for this LlamaIndex build.

blocks.title: The query engine is the product slice

spans.text: Problem anchor: a course assistant must answer from curated notes and show which LlamaIndex source nodes supported the response. The first goal is not a chat agent; it is a query engine that retrieves, cites, and refuses correctly.
The contract names allowed documents, source metadata, similarity top-k, answer style, and refusal behavior when no node supports the question.
If the expected source node for each test question is unknown, the corpus is not ready for evaluation.

blocks.analogy: Build the smallest bridge you can load-test before opening the highway.

blocks.title: Worked query-engine acceptance card

spans.text: The LlamaIndex prototype accepts a question, retrieves evidence from local Markdown notes, returns an answer with source titles, and logs retrieved chunks or nodes. It passes when four factual questions cite the expected source and the negative question refuses.

This artifact is small enough for a reviewer to inspect in one sitting, but complete enough to catch the failures that matter: missing evidence, noisy retrieval, unsupported claims, and silent fallback.

items.text: Pick three source files and record their source metadata.
Write five user-style questions with expected source titles.
Define answer, citation, and refusal requirements.
Run the slice before adding memory, chat history, or agents.

blocks.title: Build scope
blocks.prompt: Why include a negative question in the first RAG app slice?

options.text: To reduce the number of citations.
To verify the app can say there is not enough evidence instead of inventing an answer.
To avoid building retrieval.

blocks.explanation: Refusal on missing evidence is part of grounded behavior.

modules.title: Readers and node parsers create evidence units
modules.sub: LlamaIndex retrieval quality begins with documents becoming nodes.
modules.summary: Readers load data; node parsers decide the evidence units the index can retrieve.
objectives: Explain why readers and node parsers create evidence units matters for this LlamaIndex build.
Split or parse into evidence-sized units.

blocks.title: Nodes are the retrieval surface

spans.text: A LlamaIndex reader loads source material, but the node parser decides what the retriever will later select. Nodes should preserve heading path, source title, URL or path, freshness date, and permission scope.
Parsing should respect the source: headings for Markdown, table context for tabular data, and code boundaries for developer docs.
Print sample nodes with metadata before building the index; a node that cannot support a citation should not be embedded yet.

blocks.analogy: The loader stamps the passport each chunk carries through the app.

blocks.title: Case study: source_nodes become readable after metadata repair

spans.text: The first prototype returns citations like “Document 2,” which makes review painful. After ingestion stores human-readable titles and heading paths, the same answer becomes auditable.
No model changed; the app simply preserved provenance.

items.text: Split by source structure before token windows.
Attach title, URL/path, heading, and version metadata.
Print sample units and reject malformed ones.

blocks.title: Ingestion signal
blocks.prompt: What is the fastest way to catch bad chunking before model calls?

options.text: Raise answer temperature.
Preview the chunk or node text together with metadata.
Hide citations until production.

blocks.explanation: Inspection at ingestion catches source-shape errors early.

modules.title: Index and retriever settings shape source_nodes
modules.sub: Top-k, filters, and postprocessors decide what synthesis sees.
modules.summary: LlamaIndex retrieval choices determine which nodes reach answer synthesis.
objectives: Explain why index and retriever settings shape source_nodes matters for this LlamaIndex build.
Prompt the model with explicit evidence boundaries.

blocks.title: A query engine assembles context from nodes

spans.text: A VectorStoreIndex plus query engine can feel automatic, but the important decisions remain explicit: which index, which retriever, which filters, how many nodes, and which postprocessors or rerankers.
The source_nodes returned by a response are the main debugging artifact. They should show whether the expected evidence reached synthesis.
Compare expected node IDs with returned source_nodes before judging the final answer prose.

blocks.analogy: Do not debug the whole machine when one visible gear is slipping.

cells.text: Evidence present but answer misreads it.
UI cannot trust or render output.
Structured output, citation checks, refusal gate.

blocks.title: Debug split
blocks.prompt: The expected source is absent from retrieved evidence. Which stage should you fix first?

options.text: CSS layout.
Retrieval or ingestion, before rewriting the answer prompt.
The final citation renderer only.

blocks.explanation: The model cannot cite evidence it never receives.

modules.title: Inspect source_nodes in the runnable path
modules.sub: The first implementation should print the evidence objects.
modules.summary: A useful LlamaIndex demo returns an answer and the source nodes behind it.
objectives: Explain why inspect source_nodes in the runnable path matters for this LlamaIndex build.
Predict which source answers a test question.

blocks.title: The answer is only half the response

spans.text: The LlamaIndex response object can expose `source_nodes`. Use them. They are the bridge between retrieval evaluation and answer review.
Spaced recall: from faithfulness evaluation, a citation is only useful when the cited node supports the generated claim. Printing source_nodes makes that review possible.
Keep the initial corpus tiny enough that every source node can be inspected by hand.

blocks.title: LlamaIndex query engine with source_nodes trace
blocks.code:
from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex

DOCS = [
    Document(text="Reranking reorders retrieved candidates before generation.", metadata={"source": "retrieval.md"}),
    Document(text="Chunking preserves answer evidence with headings and metadata.", metadata={"source": "chunking.md"}),
]

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(DOCS)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=2)
response = query_engine.query("What does reranking do before generation?")

print(response)
for node in response.source_nodes:
    print("TRACE", node.metadata, node.score, node.text[:80])
blocks.explanation: The LlamaIndex path builds an index and prints source nodes, which is the minimum evidence loop to review.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it with dependencies installed, predict which source node should be most relevant.
predictThenReveal.answer: retrieval.md should be the supporting source. If not, inspect node text, metadata, top-k, and embedding behavior.

blocks.title: Runnable slice
blocks.prompt: Why use a tiny corpus for the first implementation?

options.text: Tiny corpora prove production scalability.
It makes retrieval and citation failures easy to inspect by hand.
It removes the need for metadata.

blocks.explanation: Small slices are for correctness and observability, not scale claims.

modules.title: Evaluate before wrapping the query engine as a tool
modules.sub: Agents should use a reliable query engine, not repair it.
modules.summary: LlamaIndex agents and workflows should sit on top of a tested retrieval layer.
objectives: Explain why evaluate before wrapping the query engine as a tool matters for this LlamaIndex build.

blocks.title: Do not hide weak retrieval inside an agent

spans.text: If the query engine misses expected source nodes for direct questions, wrapping it in a FunctionAgent or workflow will not solve the evidence problem. It will just make the failure harder to read.
The gate should include source-node hit rate, faithful answer review, negative-case refusal, and metadata/citation quality. Only then should the query engine become an agent tool.
The next complexity step is allowed only when the simple query path passes.

blocks.title: Release gate for a LlamaIndex query engine

spans.text: Use this checklist before calling the build complete.

items.text: The retrieved evidence contains the facts stated in the answer.
Each citation points to a readable source title and location.
The negative test produces a qualified refusal or “not enough evidence.”
The trace shows retrieved IDs, scores or ranks, and final packed context.
The acceptance test reruns after source, model, framework, or chunking changes.

blocks.title: Release gate
blocks.prompt: What should block release even if the answer sounds helpful?

options.text: The trace includes too many useful details for developers.
A factual claim that is not supported by the retrieved cited evidence.
The app has only one model provider.

blocks.explanation: Groundedness is the top-level promise of a RAG app.

prototype.label: Prototype
prototype.laymanDefinition: A small working version used to prove the workflow and failure cases.
prototype.technicalNote: A useful AI prototype includes representative inputs, acceptance checks, observability, and known limits rather than only a happy-path demo.

retriever.label: Retriever
retriever.laymanDefinition: The component that finds relevant evidence before the model answers.
retriever.technicalNote: Retrievers need chunking, metadata filters, ranking, citation handoff, and evaluation against real questions.

validator.label: Validator
validator.laymanDefinition: A check that decides whether an output or workflow step meets the contract.
validator.technicalNote: Validators can inspect schemas, citations, safety rules, acceptance tests, and regressions before a result reaches users.

trace.label: Trace
trace.laymanDefinition: A recorded path of model calls, retrieval, tools, tokens, latency, and errors.
trace.technicalNote: Traces make build lessons debuggable by showing which prompt, source, tool, model, and check produced a result.

deployment.label: Deployment
deployment.laymanDefinition: The packaged path that serves the workflow to real users or reviewers.
deployment.technicalNote: Deployment includes environment, secrets, routing, monitoring, rollback, and data-handling policy, not just pushing code.

acceptance_test.label: Acceptance test
acceptance_test.laymanDefinition: A concrete test that says the feature is good enough for the intended use.
acceptance_test.technicalNote: Acceptance tests should cover the target scenario, expected artifact, failure mode, and evidence needed for review.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: You pin the query-engine contract at the start of a LlamaIndex build. What is the PRIMARY reason for doing this before writing any code?

options.text: It lets you choose the fastest embedding model for your hardware.
It forces you to define what a correct answer and a correct refusal look like, so every later decision has a measurable target.
It automatically generates test documents from your corpus.
It locks the LlamaIndex version so dependencies don't drift.

questions.explanation: Pinning the contract first means you agree on answer and refusal behavior upfront, giving every subsequent build decision a concrete pass/fail criterion.

questions.prompt: A reader ingests a 40-page PDF and a node parser splits it into chunks. Which outcome best describes what these two steps produce together?

options.text: A single embedding vector representing the whole document.
A ranked list of the most relevant sentences in the document.
A set of evidence-sized units (nodes) that can each be independently retrieved and cited.
A compressed summary stored in the vector index.

questions.explanation: Readers load raw content and node parsers split it into retrieval-ready chunks — the granular units the retriever can fetch and the LLM can cite individually.

questions.prompt: In LlamaIndex, what does the `source_nodes` field on a query response tell you, and why does inspecting it matter during development?
questions.acceptableAnswer: `source_nodes` lists the specific document chunks (nodes) the retriever selected to answer the query. Inspecting it lets you verify that the right evidence was retrieved, catch cases where irrelevant or missing chunks were used, and confirm that citations in the generated answer actually map to real retrieved content.
questions.explanation: `source_nodes` is the retriever's evidence trail — checking it is the only way to confirm the model's answer is grounded in the documents you indexed, not hallucinated.

questions.prompt: You change `similarity_top_k` from 2 to 6 in your retriever settings. What is the most likely trade-off?

options.text: The index rebuilds faster but uses more disk space.
The LLM receives more candidate evidence, which can improve recall but may dilute precision and increase token cost.
Refusal behavior is disabled because the model always finds something to cite.
Node parsing is re-triggered automatically to match the new value.

questions.explanation: A higher `similarity_top_k` widens the evidence window — useful for complex queries, but it risks including loosely relevant nodes and raises prompt token usage.

questions.prompt: Before wrapping your query engine as a tool for an agent, you run a citation evaluation pass. A claim in the generated answer has NO matching span in any `source_node`. What should you do?

options.text: Accept the answer — the model's parametric knowledge is a valid fallback.
Increase the chunk size so each node contains more text.
Treat it as a hallucination signal: debug the retriever or prompt, and do not ship until citations are grounded.
Switch to a larger LLM, which is less likely to fabricate.

questions.explanation: An unsupported claim means the answer is not grounded in your documents; shipping it as a tool would propagate hallucinations downstream — fix retrieval or the prompt before wrapping.
